![Completed vector path](images/c2/c2bcb1d71d99d24ae325386c8b99146b5854c6186b0f25ce64bfe24cf8379ef8.png)

Construct a route $O\to X\to C$ whose first segment is parallel to $\mathbf{b}$ and whose second segment is parallel to $\mathbf{a}$. The added dashed lines show this route.

A copy of $\mathbf{b}$ moves one square right and two squares up. The segment from $O$ to $X$ moves three squares right and six squares up, so $OX=3|\mathbf{b}|$ with the same direction. Thus $\overrightarrow{OX}=3\mathbf{b}$.

A copy of $\mathbf{a}$ moves two squares right and one square up. From $X$ to $C$, move four squares left and two squares down. The length is $2|\mathbf{a}|$, but the direction is opposite, so $\overrightarrow{XC}=-2\mathbf{a}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{c}&=\overrightarrow{OX}+\overrightarrow{XC}\\
&=3\mathbf{b}-2\mathbf{a}\\
&=-2\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Because $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are not parallel, this expression is unique. Match each coefficient to its vector, rather than to the order of travel: $\lambda=-2$ and $\mu=3$.

Consider the picture above. Given that $\mathbf{l}=\lambda \mathbf{j}+\mu \mathbf{k}$, find $\lambda $ and $\mu .$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/6c/6c9273c0b89d4c06c8a8591b8e8e94b0c83b2d1d4bd04b64ed8cb0a185619b5f.png)

In $△OJL$ shown above, we have 

- $OJ=|\mathbf{j}|$

- $\overset{\to }{OJ}$ has the opposite direction to $\mathbf{j}$

Hence, $\overset{\to }{OJ}=-\mathbf{j}.$

Similarly:

- $JL=2|\mathbf{k}|$

- $\overset{\to }{JL}$ has the opposite direction to $\mathbf{k}$

Hence, $\overset{\to }{JL}=-2\mathbf{k}.$

Additionally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{l} & =\overset{\to }{OJ}+\overset{\to }{JL} \\  & =-\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $\mathbf{l}=\lambda \mathbf{j}+\mu \mathbf{k}=-\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k}.$

Since $\mathbf{j}∦\mathbf{k},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

- $\lambda =-1$ and $\mu =-2$

$$

![Completed vector path](images/be/be23bdf90ef85ad1d8b373ca25d9112b6d574c316f729c90db4269bdc3984147.png)

Draw a path $O\to X\to C$, first parallel to $\mathbf{a}$ and then parallel to $\mathbf{b}$, as shown.

From $O$ to $X$, move three squares down. The vector $\mathbf{a}$ moves two squares up, so $OX=\frac{3}{2}|\mathbf{a}|$ and the directions are opposite. Hence $\overrightarrow{OX}=-\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}$.

From $X$ to $C$, move four squares right and two squares up. This is twice the displacement of $\mathbf{b}$, in the same direction, so $\overrightarrow{XC}=2\mathbf{b}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{c}&=\overrightarrow{OX}+\overrightarrow{XC}\\
&=-\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The two reference vectors are not parallel, so matching coefficients gives $\lambda=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $\mu=2$. The negative sign records the downward part of the route; a length ratio alone does not give its sign.
